Field surveys of Coldwater crayfish (Orconectes eupunctus) in the Eleven Point River system have revealed that newly extruded eggs, measuring approximately 2.2 mm in diameter, produce hatchlings with a remarkably low wet weight at birth of only 0.0056 grams [Wwb = 0.0056 grams]. This minute neonatal mass is typical of crayfish species that rely heavily on yolk reserves during the early lecithotrophic larval phase. As the juvenile crustaceans grow and undergo successive molts, they gradually approach the size threshold associated with the onset of gonadal activity. Morphometric analyses indicate that the total length at puberty is approximately 1.3 centimeters [Lp = approximately 1.3 centimeters], a size commonly attained during the second growing season in populations inhabiting Ozark spring-fed streams. This pubertal length corresponds to a wet weight at puberty of about 0.622 grams [Wwp = about 0.622 grams], representing a substantial increase from the initial hatchling mass. The transition from an immature individual to a reproductively viable organism thus involves more than a hundredfold increase in wet mass, reflecting the intense somatic investment required during the juvenile crustacean stage before the first mating can occur.

Populations of Coldwater crayfish occupying stable thermal regimes typical of groundwater-fed tributaries exhibit a consistent pattern of maximum adult size. The ultimate carapace length, measured from the tip of the rostrum to the posterior margin of the cephalothorax, reaches 2.0 centimeters [Li = 2.0 centimeters] in fully grown individuals from these habitats, a modest dimension compared to several sympatric congeners and likely constrained by the cool, nutrient-poor conditions of Ozark headwater streams. This carapace dimension serves as a reliable predictor of overall body proportions and is frequently used by field ecologists to estimate reproductive potential and competitive ability within the benthic community. At this maximum structural size, the corresponding ultimate wet weight attained by adults is 2.45 grams [Wwi = 2.45 grams], a value derived from length-mass regressions calibrated against local specimens. This adult body mass represents the culmination of several years of intermittent growth punctuated by ecdysis, after which further increases in carapace dimensions become negligible. The attainment of this asymptotic mass signals the transition into the mature, ovigerous adult crustacean phase, during which energetic resources are increasingly directed toward the production of broods rather than continued somatic expansion.

Longevity estimates for Orconectes eupunctus have been derived from mark-recapture studies conducted in thermally buffered spring runs. Under controlled laboratory conditions maintained at a constant temperature of 20 °C [T = 20 °C], the maximum lifespan is approximately 1,460 days [am = approximately 1,460 days], a duration comparable to that reported for the related species Orconectes limosus. This duration places the Coldwater crayfish among the shorter-lived members of the genus, a pattern that may reflect the energetic constraints imposed by the species' specialized headwater habitat. Field observations corroborate this estimate, as the oldest recaptured individuals from the wild typically fall within the third or fourth year following their initial marking as young-of-the-year. The completion of the lifespan is often preceded by a period of reproductive senescence, during which ovigerous females produce progressively smaller clutches before natural mortality eventually occurs. Seasonal temperature fluctuations in the natural environment may slightly modulate this laboratory-derived figure, but the 20 °C [T = 20 °C] regime is considered representative of the optimal thermal conditions experienced during the active growing months.

Reproductive output in Coldwater crayfish is tightly linked to female body size, with larger individuals contributing disproportionately to recruitment. Berried females attach their fertilised ova to the pleopods, where the embryonated eggs undergo development over several weeks. The minimum size at which females first become ovigerous is constrained by the pubertal length of 1.3 cm [Lp = 1.3 cm], although most first-time breeders are slightly larger. Fecundity per reproductive event is modest, with early-stage broods typically containing between 15 and 30 eggs per clutch [N_R_i = between 15 and 30 eggs per clutch], depending on maternal body condition and local food availability. Given that females in this system produce only a single clutch each year [F_R_i = single clutch each year] due to the short growing season in their cool-water habitat, annual reproductive output is relatively low compared to many other cambarid crayfishes. This infrequent reproductive schedule may be an adaptation to the resource-limited conditions of Ozark headwater streams, where surplus energy for gametogenesis is accumulated slowly. The trade-off between clutch size and frequency appears to favor investment per individual offspring rather than maximizing the total number of young.

Comparisons between the life history traits of Orconectes eupunctus and those of sympatric crayfishes reveal several distinctive features. Whereas related congeners often exceed an adult body mass of several grams, the Coldwater crayfish reaches an ultimate wet weight of only 2.45 grams [Wwi = 2.45 grams], placing it among the smaller members of the regional crayfish fauna. This modest adult size is accompanied by the correspondingly small wet weight at puberty of 0.622 grams [Wwp = 0.622 grams], a value that underscores the species' abbreviated growth trajectory before the onset of reproductive activity. The ultimate carapace length of 2.0 centimeters [Li = 2.0 centimeters] is similarly reduced relative to that of the more widespread Orconectes species occupying downstream reaches. These constrained size metrics are likely linked to the species' thermal environment: the consistent spring-fed temperatures of approximately 20 °C [T = 20 °C] during the active season limit the duration of the growth window and may depress the maximum attainable body dimensions. From an ecological perspective, the small body size and low wet weight at birth of 0.0056 grams [Wwb = 0.0056 grams] suggest that juvenile mortality is high, necessitating a compensatory investment in egg production despite the modest per-clutch output.
